related_questions.question: What are the four stages of congestive heart failure?

text_blocks.snippet: The American College of Cardiology (ACC) and American Heart Association (AHA) classify congestive heart failure (CHF) into four stages: A, B, C, and D. These stages represent a progression from high risk of developing heart failure to advanced, end-stage heart failure.
Here's a breakdown of the stages:

list.title: Stage A (At Risk):
list.snippet: Individuals are at high risk of developing heart failure due to conditions like hypertension, diabetes, or family history, but they have no structural heart disease or symptoms.

list.title: Stage B (Pre-Heart Failure):
list.snippet: Structural heart disease is present, but the individual has not yet experienced symptoms of heart failure.

list.title: Stage C (Symptomatic Heart Failure):
list.snippet: Structural heart disease is present, and the individual experiences symptoms of heart failure, such as shortness of breath or fatigue.

list.title: Stage D (Advanced Heart Failure):
list.snippet: Advanced symptoms persist despite treatment, and the individual may require specialized interventions like heart transplants or mechanical circulatory support.

text_blocks.snippet: COVID-19 can cause various heart problems, including myocardial injury, arrhythmia, and pericarditis, even in individuals with mild cases. These issues can arise during or after a COVID-19 infection.
Specific heart conditions associated with COVID-19:

list.title: Myocardial injury:
list.snippet: Damage to the heart muscle, potentially causing chest pain, shortness of breath, and swelling in the lower extremities, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

list.title: Arrhythmia:
list.snippet: Inflammation can disrupt the heart's electrical signals, leading to irregular heartbeats.

list.title: Pericarditis:
list.snippet: Inflammation of the membrane surrounding the heart, which can cause chest pain and fluid buildup around the heart, says the Cleveland Clinic.

list.title: Long-term heart and lung changes:
list.snippet: Some studies suggest COVID-19 can lead to long-term changes in the heart and lungs, potentially increasing the risk of heart failure, valvular heart disease, and pulmonary hypertension.
The long-term impact of COVID-19 on the cardiovascular system is still being studied, according to Mount Sinai.
Even individuals with mild COVID-19 cases can experience heart problems.
If you experience any new or concerning symptoms, particularly chest pain or shortness of breath, after a COVID-19 infection, seek medical advice promptly.
